solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Holding carbon, a scholar prepared sketches

indicators.note: holding something means having it inside, so one piece sits within the other
prepared suggests letters worked up into a new form, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: C is the chemical symbol for carbon
taken as written

explanation.surface: A student working on carbon-based drawing materials gets some sketches ready.
explanation.walkthrough: The C sits among the shuffled letters of A SCHOLAR, which together rearrange into CHARCOALS.
explanation.definitionFit: Charcoals are drawings made with sticks of charred wood, a common kind of artist's sketch.

clue.text: Letter from prisoner carried by boy soldier

indicators.note: in a down entry, something carried by another sits on top of it, so the first piece comes above the rest

blocks.note: con is slang for a convict
a son is a boy
a soldier ant is a caste of ant, so ant stands for soldier

explanation.surface: A boy soldier brings home a letter written by a prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' looks like correspondence, but it means a letter of the alphabet; soldier giving ANT is a crossword staple from the soldier ant.
explanation.definitionFit: A consonant is any alphabet character that is not a vowel, so it is a kind of letter.

clue.text: A third character in wardrobe, and second one on wardrobe

indicators.note: the third character of a word is its third letter, so just that one is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the third letter of the first wardrobe
mo is short for moment, as in 'wait a mo'
I is the Roman numeral for one
re means on or about, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: A puzzling instruction about letters, read as if counting characters printed in and on a wardrobe.
explanation.walkthrough: The first wardrobe is raw material; only the second is the definition. Second gives MO, one gives I, and on gives RE.
explanation.definitionFit: An armoire is a tall cupboard for clothes, the French-derived name for a wardrobe.

clue.text: One in Police Academy film carrying around diamonds

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece carrying others has them on top of it, so it comes last

blocks.note: ca is short for circa, meaning around
D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds
E.T. is Spielberg's film about an extra-terrestrial

explanation.surface: A character in the Police Academy comedy films is seen holding diamonds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Police Academy film' looks like one unit, but the film is the separate ET; the definition stops at Academy.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadet is a trainee at a police or military academy, so one enrolled there is a cadet.

clue.text: A clergyman served egg eats 100?! That's right

indicators.note: what eats something takes it inside, so a piece goes into the middle of the other letters

blocks.note: taken as written
a nod to the curate's egg, the Punch cartoon of a curate served a bad egg; the clergyman is a curate
C is the Roman numeral for 100

explanation.surface: A churchman given an egg wolfs down a hundred of them, and someone confirms it.
explanation.walkthrough: The curate's egg is the famous Victorian cartoon of a curate politely saying his bad egg is good in parts. A + CURATE takes in C after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Accurate means correct or exact, which is what right means when confirming something.

clue.text: Spiritual healer and phoney bloke sharing money

indicators.note: two words sharing a letter use it only once, so one copy drops out where they meet

blocks.note: a sham is a fake
a bloke is a man
M is an abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: A spiritual healer and a fraudster split the takings between them.
explanation.walkthrough: SHAM ends in M and MAN begins with it, so the two overlap on one M to make SHAMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaman is a figure in many traditional cultures who heals and mediates with the spirit world.

clue.text: Top players understand both sides of darts

indicators.note: the two sides of a word are its outermost letters, so only those are kept

blocks.note: to see is to understand, as in 'I see'
the first and last letters of darts

explanation.surface: The best competitors grasp the game of darts from end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: In a tournament the top players are seeded, so the strongest entrants are called seeds.

clue.text: In parts of the home counties, good husbands tend new leaves

indicators.note: here leaves is the verb, departs, so a letter goes out of the word before it

blocks.note: the Home Counties surround London in the South East of England
G is the abbreviation for good
husbands are men
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Around London, decent husbands look after the fresh leaves in their gardens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like foliage to be tended, but it is a verb: N departs from TEND. The Home Counties are the counties surrounding London.
explanation.definitionFit: Something segmented is divided into sections, so it exists in parts.

clue.text: Omission of badly-written lines crowding the contents of biog

indicators.note: badly written words are garbled, so their letters come out in a new order
the contents of a word are what lies inside it, so its first and last letters are dropped
to crowd something is to press in around it, so the other letters enclose it

blocks.note: taken as written
the inner two letters of biog

explanation.surface: A biography is marred by sloppy lines that crowd out its proper contents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly-written lines' looks like a description of the biog's prose, but lines is simply the raw letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Elision is the leaving out of a sound or syllable in speech, a kind of omission.

clue.text: One captivated by kids' programme?

indicators.note: something captivated is held captive, so the letters are held inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of kids and the start of programme

explanation.surface: Who is enthralled by a children's television show?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: the word sits inside 'kids' programme', and the one glued to such a show is a small child.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprog is British slang for a young child, the natural viewer enthralled by children's television.

clue.text: Travelling from Northern Europe, heads of murderous armies usurp Rome's capital

indicators.note: the heads of words are their first letters, so only those are kept
to usurp is to seize another's place, so new letters push out an old one
a capital is the letter at the head of a word, so just the first is meant

blocks.note: Nordic describes Scandinavia and its neighbours
the first letters of these two words
the first letter of Rome

explanation.surface: Murderous armies sweep south from Scandinavia and seize Rome, like the barbarian invasions.
explanation.walkthrough: MA takes the place of the R in NORDIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomadic people move from place to place rather than settling, so they are always travelling.

clue.text: Increasingly irritated as a result of broken earring

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces that can be put back in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone grows more and more annoyed because their earring has snapped.
explanation.definitionFit: Angrier is the comparative of angry, so it means more irritated than before.

clue.text: Belt out Billy Idol's number ones

indicators.note: number ones are the firsts in line, so the first letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the first letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Sing loudly the chart-topping hits of the punk star Billy Idol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belt out' reads as one verb, singing loudly, but Belt is the definition and out supplies the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An obi is the broad sash worn around the waist with a Japanese kimono, a kind of belt.

clue.text: Frightening article worn by rector put away

indicators.note: something worn by a person goes around them, so it wraps the letters that follow

blocks.note: an article is an object or thing
R is the abbreviation for rector
put away food means eaten it

explanation.surface: A vicar is wearing some alarming garment that ought to be stored out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' tempts the solver toward the grammatical THE or A, but here it is an object, in the sense of an article of clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Threatening and frightening both describe something menacing that causes fear.

clue.text: Lads stripped before match to get fit

indicators.note: stripping removes the outer covering, so only the inner letters remain
before places one piece ahead of the next in the answer

blocks.note: the inner letters of lads
to equate two things is to match them

explanation.surface: Footballers change and train before a game to get in shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' looks like physical fitness, but here it means suitable or good enough.
explanation.definitionFit: Adequate means suitable or sufficient, the sense of fit in 'fit for purpose'.

clue.text: Comprehensive article in Le Figaro on Ravel is rewritten

indicators.note: rewritten words are set down afresh, so their letters can take a new order

blocks.note: un is the French indefinite article, as found in a French newspaper
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wide-ranging piece in the French newspaper Le Figaro reassesses the composer Ravel.
explanation.walkthrough: Le Figaro is a French daily, which signals French: its article is UN. The word 'is' belongs to the fodder, not the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Universal means applying to all cases or everyone, which is what comprehensive means.

clue.text: Attitudes concerning women getting ejected from golf course?

indicators.note: what is ejected from a place is thrown out of it, so these letters are removed

blocks.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading
W is the abbreviation for women
St Andrews in Scotland is the most famous golf course in the world

explanation.surface: Views on whether women should be thrown off a traditionally male golf club.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that golf course stands for one particular course: St Andrews, the old home of golf on Scotland's east coast. Take out RE and W.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand is a position taken on an issue, so stands are attitudes or stated views.

clue.text: Pick league's top 2 within division

indicators.note: the top two of a word in a down clue are its first two letters
within puts one piece inside another

blocks.note: a section is a division
the first two letters of league

explanation.surface: Choose which teams from the top of the league go into each division.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'top' means the start of a word, so top 2 is its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A selection is a choice, which is what a pick is as a noun.

clue.text: Spirited Russian, with 5-0 crushing, goes ahead of American

indicators.note: to crush something is to squeeze it from both sides, so it ends up held in the middle
what goes ahead comes first, so the following piece is added at the end

blocks.note: V is the Roman numeral for 5 and 0 looks like the letter O
Igor is a typical Russian name
US abbreviates the United States, so means American

explanation.surface: A lively Russian side wins five-nil and goes past the American team.
explanation.walkthrough: The scoreline reads as football, but the digits become letters: 5 is a Roman numeral and 0 passes for the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Vigorous means full of energy and force, which is what spirited means.

clue.text: Wimbledon champion returning with the wrong end of racket — he's good at this!

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that is kept
having the wrong one means the proper letter has been swapped for another
returning means going back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Jannik Sinner won the men's singles at Wimbledon in 2025
the last letter of racket

explanation.surface: The Wimbledon champion comes back, his racket the wrong way round, and still excels at the game.
explanation.walkthrough: SINNER gets the wrong end: its final R becomes T, giving SINNET, which is then read backwards. The definition points back to the champion himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinner is a champion at tennis, so the game he excels at is the answer, defined by example.

clue.text: Abandon maniac electing to spurn institute

indicators.note: to spurn is to reject, so a letter is turned away and left out
something maniac is wild and crazy, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
I is the abbreviation for institute

explanation.surface: Give up on a madman who chooses to snub the institute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maniac' looks like a noun, the person electing, but it works as an adjective telling us to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To neglect something is to fail to look after it, effectively abandoning it.

clue.text: Turn, turn… I'm turning left twice

definitions.note: verb: to whirl the arms round like the sails of a mill

indicators.note: turning around makes something face the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to wind is to turn, as with a handle
taken as written
L for left, written out twice

explanation.surface: A dizzy dance: turn, turn, and spin to the left two times.
explanation.walkthrough: Every turn in the clue seems to be the same instruction; the first is the definition, the second gives WIND, and turning flips I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: To windmill is to rotate the arms in big circles like a mill's sails, so it means turn.

clue.text: One performing in Madness when heavy metal became popular?

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
rage is a kind of madness or fury
a performer is on stage

explanation.surface: A musician playing in the ska band Madness at the time heavy metal music took off.
explanation.walkthrough: Madness was a British ska-pop band, and heavy metal sounds like a music genre; here it is iron, the metal that gave an era its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iron Age is the prehistoric era when iron tools and weapons came into common use.

clue.text: Seats located among numerous tall sunflowers

indicators.note: something located among other things sits within them, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of numerous through tall to the start of sunflowers

explanation.surface: Garden benches are tucked in among a mass of towering sunflowers.
explanation.definitionFit: The stalls are the seats on the ground floor of a theatre, nearest the stage.

clue.text: Ousting the leaders of elitist splinter group spreading false insinuations

indicators.note: the leaders of words are the letters at their front, so first letters are kept
false means not genuine, so the letters are faked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letters of these four words

explanation.surface: Having pushed out its leaders, a snobbish breakaway faction spreads untrue rumours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ousting the leaders' reads as one idea, removing letters, but Ousting is fodder and the leaders are kept, not lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Suggestions can be hints or implications, which is what insinuations are, usually unpleasant ones.

clue.text: Cry out, moving up and down?

indicators.note: moving up means some letters shift to a higher place, so the order changes

blocks.note: to shout is to cry out

explanation.surface: Yell while bobbing up and down.
explanation.walkthrough: In this down entry the OUT of SHOUT climbs above the H. The definition is fair because south is down on a map, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: On a conventional map north is at the top, so south is the direction that points down the page.

clue.text: Save money by investing millions in waste management facility

indicators.note: to invest in its old sense is to clothe or surround, so one piece is wrapped in another

blocks.note: a skip is a large open bin for building rubbish, a British word for a dumpster
M is the abbreviation for millions

explanation.surface: Cut costs by sinking millions into a rubbish-processing plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Investing' looks like finance, matching save money and millions, but it means putting inside. A skip is the British name for a builder's rubbish container.
explanation.definitionFit: To skimp is to economise by spending or using less than is needed.

clue.text: Brutish monster with clubs going after soldiers

indicators.note: going after means following, so this piece comes second

blocks.note: OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs

explanation.surface: A savage beast wielding clubs chases down troops.
explanation.walkthrough: Clubs reads as weapons in a monster's hands, but it is the card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: An orc is a brutal goblin-like creature from fantasy fiction, notably Tolkien.

clue.text: In audition, you listen out for instrument

indicators.note: an audition is a hearing, so a word is taken by its sound
out here means disordered, as in put out, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letter U is said just like you
taken as written

explanation.surface: A judge at a music audition tells you to listen out for a particular instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: Instrument looks musical given audition, but here it is a tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A utensil is a tool or implement, especially for the kitchen, and instrument can mean a tool.

clue.text: Paperwork — Solomon's first social security payment — is on the counter

indicators.note: counter means contrary, against the usual direction, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Solomon is the setter, so Solomon is becomes I am, shortened
A is first, as in A1 or grade A
a giro was a British fortnightly benefit cheque

explanation.surface: The setter fills in forms for his first welfare cheque at the post office counter.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's name stands for I. 'Paperwork' looks like admin, but it is paper folding.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into shapes, literally work done with paper.

clue.text: Bangladesh's eastern border as designated by NATO

definitions.text: Bangladesh's eastern border as designated by NATO

blocks.note: surface reading: the frontier along the east side of the country
setter's reading: the eastern edge of the word Bangladesh is its last letter, and NATO's phonetic alphabet has a code word for that letter

explanation.surface: A geopolitical note on how the military alliance labels Bangladesh's eastern frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: Eastern border means the last letter of the word, H, and NATO's spelling alphabet calls H Hotel.
explanation.definitionFit: In the NATO phonetic alphabet used by radio operators, each letter has a code word, and H is spoken as this one.

clue.text: Hip essay about the ending of Dylan's 'Like a Rolling Stone'?

indicators.note: about suggests moving around, so the letters are turned into a new order
the ending of a word is its last letter, so just that is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the last letter of Dylan

explanation.surface: A trendy essay about the closing lines of Bob Dylan's song 'Like a Rolling Stone'.
explanation.walkthrough: The song title is the definition, read literally: Sisyphus was condemned to roll a boulder uphill forever.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisyphean describes endless futile labour, after Sisyphus, who forever rolled a stone up a hill.
